title: The Firefly Jar Rescue
markdown:
Rill, Vale, and Ember met where they always met, under the Whispering Willow by the marsh path. The willow’s long leaves clicked softly in the late light. Rill’s nose worked the air as if trouble had a scent of its own. Vale’s sleek fur already held a fidget. Ember stood between them with both paws around a glass jar.

Inside the jar, fireflies from the Whisperwind Peaks ticked from colour to colour — rose, then gold, then a tired grey. Their light had been thinning since noon.

“Professor Hoot needs them at the marsh observatory,” Ember said. “His star-charting lantern will not hold without them, and he has to find the Moonpetal Meadows tonight.”

Rill measured the sun against the willow. “Half a day’s walk, and the day is already leaning over.”

Vale bounced on his toes. “I know a shortcut through the Whispering Woods. We can beat the dark.”

Rill’s ears tipped back. Shortcuts, in her experience, were arguments the woods liked to win. She nearly said they should keep to the marsh path they knew. Ember’s jar pulsed once, weakly, and that decided her more than Vale’s bounce. They had to move. She would watch the thorns.

They left the willow and crossed into the woods. The air changed at once: closer, greener, full of small rustles that might have been mice or only leaves. Vale darted ahead into a thicket that looked quicker than the bend in the path.

“This way,” he called.

“Vale, wait,” Rill said. “Those thorns are set like hooks. And something is moving in there.”

He did not wait. Saving time, he believed, was the same as helping. A yelp cut the thicket. Then a frantic rustle. Then nothing at all.

“Vale?” Ember’s voice went thin.

Vale tumbled out wrapped in vines, looking like a kite that had lost an argument with a hedge. Worse, he had clipped Ember on the way. The jar slipped, rolled, nudged a loose stone, and rode the stone down an embankment into a pocket of wet mud. The glass did not break. The mud sealed it. The fireflies’ colours flattened to a dull smear.

Ember scrambled after it. “Oh, no.” He turned the jar in his paws. The insects inside flickered as if they were trying to see through a closed eyelid.

Vale’s ears dropped. “I did not mean to. I only wanted us there sooner.”

Rill hopped close enough that her whiskers brushed his shoulder. “We all rush. The question is what we do with the mud.” She studied the glass. “These fireflies keep their own light only while they can see the sky. If we leave them blind, they will fade before we reach Hoot.”

The sun slipped another notch. Ember’s frown deepened. “If we cannot clean it soon, they may not last the observatory, let alone the meadows.”

Vale’s mistake sat between them like a third companion. Rill turned toward the stream that cut the woods and pointed with one paw. “Smooth-leafed watercress. It lifts dirt from thin things without scratching. And those pebbles are worn enough to polish, not gouge.”

Vale swallowed. “I will fetch the watercress. Carefully, this time.”

“I will choose the pebbles,” Rill said. “Ember, hold the jar as if it were an egg.”

They worked at the stream’s edge. Vale moved as if each stem might accuse him. Rill picked stones that had no sharp lip. Ember’s paws trembled, but the jar stayed level. Together they rubbed the mud away in small circles, watercress first, then the cool stones. It was slow. It had to be. The last smear left the glass, and the fireflies found the sky again. Colour came back through them in a rush — not a show, only a pulse that meant they could work.

“They’re themselves again,” Ember whispered.

Vale let out a breath he had been storing since the thicket. “I am sorry. I will keep to the path we can see.”

“You looked before you picked the cress,” Rill said. “That is the part that counts. Now we run, and we run the long way on purpose.”

They did. Vale scouted, then checked over his shoulder instead of vanishing. Rill chose the firm ground. Ember carried the jar like a captured sunset, close to his chest. In the Meadow of Murmurs the grasses spoke around their ankles. An owl called once. A fox’s eyes held them from the ditch and let them pass. They did not stop to be interesting.

The marsh observatory rose as the last rim of sun went under: a slender wooden tower with a lamp-room already dark. They took the steps two at a time.

Professor Hoot, a great grey owl in spectacles too wide for dignity, blinked at the three of them and then at the jar. “Ah. You have made the hour, and not a minute more.”

Ember set the fireflies in his wings. Their light filled the lamp-room in a steady wash. Hoot fitted the jar into the lantern’s cradle. “This will hold. With it I can chart the meadows before the moon climbs too high.”

They did not linger for praise. On the walk back, Vale stayed on the marsh path even when a tempting gap opened in the trees. Under the Whispering Willow again, he sat where they had started and flicked a burr from his fur without making a joke of it.

Rill’s whiskers eased. The willow clicked in the first night air. Ember’s empty paws still remembered the jar’s weight. They had brought the light where it was needed, and they had brought Vale back by a route he could name.
characters: Rill (a riverbank bunny), Vale (a young stoat), Ember (a firefly collector)
